transcription.tex: (b) Prove by induction that\[(1+i)^n=2^{n/2}e^{in\pi/4},\quad n\in\mathbb Z^+.\]

True for \(n=1\). Assume true for \(n=k\). Then\[\begin{aligned}(1+i)^{k+1}&=(1+i)2^{k/2}e^{ik\pi/4}\\&=2^{(k+1)/2}e^{i(k+1)\pi/4}.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus it holds for \(k+1\), so for every positive integer by induction.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Challenge 1B}\par (a) Prove by induction, for positive integers \(n\),\[(re^{i\theta})^n=r^ne^{in\theta}.\]\par Use only the complex multiplication rule, not an assumed law of indices.
True for \(n=1\). Assume true for \(k\).\[(re^{i\theta})^{k+1}=re^{i\theta}\,r^ke^{ik\theta}\]\[=r^{k+1}e^{i(k+1)\theta}.\]\par Hence true for all positive integers by induction.

transcription.tex: Prove the result by induction for positive integers \(n\).\par \textbf{Edexcel FP2 June 2013 · Q4}

True for \(n=1\). Assume true for \(n=k\). Multiplying by \(z\), the product rule gives\[z^{k+1}=r^{k+1}[\cos(k\theta+\theta)\]\[{}+i\sin(k\theta+\theta)].\]\par This is the result for \(k+1\); therefore true for all positive integers.

Alternatively, expand the product using the angle-addition identities:\[\cos k\theta\cos\theta-\sin k\theta\sin\theta=\cos(k+1)\theta,\]\[\sin k\theta\cos\theta+\cos k\theta\sin\theta=\sin(k+1)\theta.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 1C · Question 9}\par Use De Moivre’s theorem to show that\[(a+bi)^n+(a-bi)^n\]\par is real for integer \(n\), wherever the powers are defined.

Write \(a+bi=re^{i\theta}\), so \(a-bi=re^{-i\theta}\).\[\begin{aligned}(a+bi)^n+(a-bi)^n&=r^n(e^{in\theta}+e^{-in\theta})\\&=2r^n\cos n\theta,\end{aligned}\]\par which is real. For negative \(n\), require \(r\ne0\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Challenge 1C}\par Without Euler’s relation, prove for positive integers \(n\) and \(r>0\):\[[r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)]^{-n}\]\[=r^{-n}[\cos(-n\theta)+i\sin(-n\theta)].\]\par You may assume De Moivre’s theorem for positive integers.

By De Moivre and the definition of a negative power,\[\frac1{r^n(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta)}.\]\par Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate:\[\frac{\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta}{r^n(\cos^2n\theta+\sin^2n\theta)}\]\[=r^{-n}[\cos(-n\theta)+i\sin(-n\theta)].\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 1D · Question 6}\par (a) Show\[\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1.\]\par (b) Find the six roots of\[32x^6-48x^4+18x^2-\frac32=0\]\par to 3 decimal places.
Compare real parts of \((c+is)^6\):\[\cos6\theta=c^6-15c^4s^2+15c^2s^4-s^6.\]\par Substitute \(s^2=1-c^2\) and simplify.

Put \(x=\cos\theta\). Then \(\cos6\theta=1/2\), so\[\theta=\pm\frac\pi{18}+\frac{k\pi}3.\]\par The six distinct values are\[\boxed{x=\pm0.985,\ \pm0.643,\ \pm0.342}.\]\par There are six distinct roots of a degree-six polynomial, so these are all the roots.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Complex geometric series}\par A geometric series starts \(w,wz,wz^2,\ldots\). The common ratio is \(z\).
\textbf{Convergence}\par The modulus measures distance from zero: \(|-4|=4\), \(|3+4i|=5\).
If \(|z|<1\), then \(z^n\to0\), and\[S_\infty=\frac{w}{1-z}.\]\par A non-zero geometric series converges precisely when the modulus of its ratio is less than 1.

slides.title: Using mod-arg form to split summation

transcription.tex: \textbf{Using modulus–argument form to split a sum}\par For \(\theta\ne2k\pi\),\[S=e^{i\theta}+e^{2i\theta}+\cdots+e^{ni\theta}\]\[=\frac{e^{i\theta}(e^{ni\theta}-1)}{e^{i\theta}-1}.\]\par The first term is \(e^{i\theta}\), common ratio \(e^{i\theta}\), and there are \(n\) terms.

Expand each exponential using Euler’s formula:\[S=(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)+\cdots\]\[{}+(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta).\]\par Group the real and imaginary parts:\[\operatorname{Re}S=\cos\theta+\cdots+\cos n\theta,\]\[\operatorname{Im}S=\sin\theta+\cdots+\sin n\theta.\]\par Thus one complex geometric sum gives both trigonometric sums.

transcription.tex: \textbf{The \(n\)th roots of unity}\[z^n=1\implies z=e^{2k\pi i/n},\quad k=0,\ldots,n-1.\]\par They are equally spaced on the unit circle, with angular separation \(2\pi/n\).\par Put \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}\). The roots are \(1,\omega,\ldots,\omega^{n-1}\).
For \(n\ge2\), show that their sum is zero.
\[1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^{n-1}=\frac{1-\omega^n}{1-\omega}=0.\]\par Here \(\omega^n=1\) and \(\omega\ne1\).\par Geometrically, the vectors are balanced around the origin.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 1F · Question 9}\par (a) Solve\[1+z+z^2+\cdots+z^7=0.\]\par (b) Hence deduce that \(z^2+1\) and \(z^4+1\) are factors of this polynomial.
At \(z=1\) the sum is 8, so \(z\ne1\). The geometric sum gives\[\frac{z^8-1}{z-1}=0.\]\par Thus the solutions are the eighth roots of unity excluding 1:\[\boxed{z=e^{ik\pi/4},\quad k=1,\ldots,7}.\]
\[z^8-1=(z-1)(z+1)(z^2+1)(z^4+1).\]\par Dividing by \(z-1\) proves both required factors. Equivalently, each root of either factor is an eighth root of unity other than 1.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Challenge}\par (a) Find the six roots of \(z^6=1\) as \(e^{i\theta}\), with principal arguments.\par (b) Hence show that the solutions of \((z+1)^6=z^6\) are\[z=-\frac12+\frac i2\cot\frac{k\pi}6,\quad k=1,\ldots,5.\]

Neither \(z=0\) nor \(z=-1\) is a solution. Put \(u=z/(z+1)\). Then \(u^6=1\), but \(u\ne1\).\par Write \(u=e^{2i\alpha}\), \(\alpha=k\pi/6\), \(k=1,\ldots,5\).\[z=\frac u{1-u}=\frac{e^{i\alpha}}{-2i\sin\alpha}\]\[=\frac{i(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha)}{2\sin\alpha}=\boxed{-\frac12+\frac i2\cot\alpha}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Roots and regular polygons}\par If \(z_1\) is one root of \(z^n=w\ne0\), all roots are\[z_1,z_1\omega,\ldots,z_1\omega^{n-1},\quad\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}.\]\par They form a regular \(n\)-gon centred at the origin.\par For example, the roots of \(z^6=7+24i\) have modulus \(25^{1/6}\) and angular separation \(\pi/3\).
Multiplication by \(\omega\) rotates a point by \(2\pi/n\) without changing its distance from the origin.\par Once one vertex is known, rotate repeatedly to generate the others.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 1G · Question 4}\par (a) Find the fourth roots of \(-12i\), as \(re^{i\theta}\) with principal arguments. Illustrate them. (6 marks)\par In increasing argument order, label them \(A,B,C,D\).\par (b) Their side midpoints are the fourth roots of a complex number \(w\). Find \(w\). (4 marks)

The roots form a square. A side midpoint has modulus \(\sqrt[4]{12}/\sqrt2=\sqrt[4]3\).\par The midpoint of \(AB\) has argument \(-3\pi/8\). Therefore\[w=\left(\sqrt[4]3e^{-3i\pi/8}\right)^4=3e^{-3i\pi/2}=\boxed{3i}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 1G · Question 5}\par A regular hexagon on an Argand diagram is centred at the origin. Vertex \(P\) represents \(8+8i\).\par Find the other five vertices in the form \(a+bi\), and illustrate them.\par Use \(z_k=(8+8i)e^{ik\pi/3}\).

For \(k=1,\ldots,5\), the vertices are\[4(1-\sqrt3)+4(1+\sqrt3)i,\]\[-4(1+\sqrt3)+4(\sqrt3-1)i,\]\[-8-8i,\]\[4(\sqrt3-1)-4(1+\sqrt3)i,\]\[4(1+\sqrt3)+4(1-\sqrt3)i.\]\par They lie on the circle of radius \(8\sqrt2\), separated by \(\pi/3\).
